title: Bytox Review: Do Hangover Patches Work? Ingredients, Evidence, Value
excerpt: An honest Bytox review: what's in the hangover patch, whether B vitamins can get through your skin, what users report, cost per night, safety, and better options.

author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest verdict first:** Bytox is a well-known hangover patch, a small adhesive sticker loaded with B vitamins that you wear on your skin while you drink. It's convenient, it's unlikely to hurt you, and plenty of buyers say they like it. But there is no good evidence that it works. Bytox hasn't published a placebo-controlled trial showing it reduces hangovers, and it hasn't published blood tests showing how much of its vitamins actually get through your skin. The basic science of skin absorption works against it, and the one study that compared vitamin patches with ordinary pills found the patch users did worse. For most people, Bytox is an expensive way to buy a feeling of being prepared.

**Who it might suit:** someone who already drinks sensibly, wants a low-effort ritual, and is happy to pay for convenience knowing the benefit may be mostly placebo. **Who should skip it:** anyone looking for something with real evidence behind it, anyone on a budget, people with sensitive skin or adhesive allergies, and anyone who might drink more because they feel "protected."

> **This is not medical advice.** This review explains general research, the brand's own descriptions, and what users commonly report. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Bytox is not an FDA-approved drug. It does not lower your blood alcohol, sober you up, or make it safe to drive. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist first if** you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have a skin condition, take prescription medicine, or are having blood work done soon (some B-vitamin products contain biotin, which can throw off certain lab tests). Seek urgent care for signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, or someone you can't wake up. In an emergency, call 911.

**About our relationship with Bytox:** we don't have an affiliate arrangement with Bytox and we don't link to their store, so we earn nothing if you buy it. We do earn a commission on two oral DHM products mentioned near the end of this review, and we say so where they appear.

## What Is Bytox?

Bytox is a US brand that sells topical patches marketed for people who drink. Its best-known product is the Bytox hangover patch, often sold under names like "Hangover Recovery Patch." You'll find it on Amazon, on the brand's own website, and in some convenience stores, bars, and festival shops. It became popular through social media and word of mouth, partly because the idea is easy to understand: stick it on before you go out, peel it off in the morning, and skip the pills.

The pitch rests on two ideas:

1. **Drinking depletes vitamins**, especially B vitamins, and topping them up should help you feel better the next day.
2. **The skin is a better route than the gut** when you've been drinking, because alcohol can interfere with how the gut absorbs nutrients.

The first idea has a grain of truth for long-term heavy drinkers, but it has little to do with a one-night hangover. The second idea is where the product runs into its biggest problem, which we'll get to shortly.

We also have a broader article on the whole product category, [Do Hangover Patches Work?](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work), which goes deeper into skin science and each vitamin. This page focuses on Bytox specifically: what you're buying, how it's meant to be used, what people report, and whether it's worth the money.

## What's in a Bytox Hangover Patch?

Bytox's hangover patch is built around a **B-vitamin complex**. Labels we've seen list the familiar B vitamins:

- **Thiamine (B1)**
- **Riboflavin (B2)**
- **Niacin (B3)**
- **Pantothenic acid (B5)**
- **Pyridoxine (B6)**
- **Biotin (B7)**
- **Folate or folic acid (B9)**
- **Cobalamin (B12)**

Some versions and some competing patches also list extras such as vitamin C, plant extracts, or antioxidants. Formulas change over time and can differ by product line and retailer, so **read the current label on the box you're buying** rather than relying on any review, including this one.

There's one important thing the label can't tell you. The amounts listed describe what's in the adhesive. They don't tell you what reaches your bloodstream. With a pill, those two numbers are reasonably close for most B vitamins. With a patch, nobody has published the second number.

## How Bytox Is Meant to Be Used

The brand's instructions are simple, and broadly similar to other vitamin patches:

- Apply the patch to **clean, dry, hair-free skin**. Common spots are the inner wrist, inner arm, upper arm, hip, or the top of the foot.
- Put it on **before you start drinking**, so it has time to work during the night.
- **Leave it on for several hours**, typically overnight, then remove it in the morning. Check the package for the exact wear time on your version.
- Use a new patch each time.

Practical tips from users are mostly about keeping it stuck on. Lotion, sweat, dancing, and showers all loosen the adhesive. Some people put it somewhere that won't rub against clothing, such as the inner arm, and press it down firmly for a few seconds after applying.

Notice what's missing from those instructions: anything about how much to drink. A patch has no effect on how quickly alcohol is absorbed or cleared, so it doesn't change your blood alcohol at all.

## Does Bytox Work? What the Evidence Says

To work, Bytox has to clear two separate hurdles. Both need to be true.

1. **Its vitamins must get through your skin in useful amounts.**
2. **Those vitamins must actually reduce hangover symptoms** once they're in your body.

There's no good evidence for either one, and there's some evidence against the first.

### Hurdle one: getting through the skin

Your skin's outer layer, called the stratum corneum, is a tough wall of flattened dead cells sealed with fats. Its job is to keep things out, and it's very good at it. Drug patches that really work, like nicotine, scopolamine (for motion sickness), fentanyl, and hormone patches, all share a few traits:

- **The molecules are small.** Dermatology researchers often cite a rough guideline called the "500 Dalton rule," proposed by Bos and Meinardi in *Experimental Dermatology* in 2000. In plain words, molecules much heavier than about 500 daltons (a unit of molecular weight) have a hard time crossing healthy skin.
- **The molecules dissolve in fat**, which lets them slip through the fatty skin barrier.
- **They work at very small doses**, so a patch can deliver enough.
- **The patch is engineered and tested** to prove a specific amount reaches the blood. That's a requirement for an approved drug patch.

B vitamins don't fit this profile well. All of them dissolve in water rather than fat. Several carry an electric charge, which makes crossing the skin even harder. And vitamin B12 is large: about 1,355 daltons, nearly three times that rough cut-off. Smaller B vitamins like niacin and B6 are under the size limit, so it's possible that small amounts get through. But "a little might get in" is very different from "this delivers a meaningful dose."

### The one study that compared patches with pills

There are no published hangover trials of vitamin patches. The most useful real-world comparison comes from a different setting. A 2019 study in the journal *Obesity Surgery* followed people after weight-loss surgery, who need lifelong vitamin supplements because their gut absorbs nutrients poorly. These patients are exactly the group a skin patch should help most. Researchers compared people using a multivitamin patch with people taking oral multivitamins over about a year. The patch users were **more likely to become deficient** in several nutrients, including vitamin D, than the people taking pills.

That study tested a different product in a different group of people, so it doesn't directly measure Bytox. But it's the best available evidence on whether vitamin patches keep vitamin levels up, and the answer was no. If a patch couldn't maintain vitamin levels in people who wore one every day for months, it's hard to see a single night making a noticeable difference.

### Hurdle two: would B vitamins fix a hangover anyway?

Suppose the vitamins did get through. Researchers don't think hangovers are mainly a vitamin shortage. The main drivers appear to be:

- **Inflammation**, as your immune system reacts to alcohol
- **Acetaldehyde**, a toxic by-product made when your liver breaks down alcohol
- **Poor sleep**, since alcohol disrupts the second half of the night
- **Dehydration and stomach irritation**
- **Congeners**, extra compounds found in darker drinks like whiskey and red wine

B vitamins don't directly address any of these. The research linking them to hangovers is thin. A 2019 survey-based study in the *Journal of Clinical Medicine* by Dutch hangover researchers (Verster and colleagues) found people with higher dietary niacin and zinc reported somewhat milder hangovers, but that's an association from food intake, not proof that a supplement helps. A small study from the 1970s found benefits from pyritinol, a synthetic relative of vitamin B6, taken in large doses by mouth. That's not the same thing as the B6 in a patch, and it hasn't been convincingly repeated.

Broad reviews of hangover remedies haven't found vitamins to be a standout. A 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ* found no compelling evidence that any remedy prevented or treated hangovers, and a 2022 systematic review in *Addiction* from researchers at the University of Bristol rated the overall evidence for hangover remedies as very low quality.

### What Bytox itself has published

As far as we're aware, Bytox has not published:

- A placebo-controlled trial of its patch for hangovers
- Blood or urine data showing how much of each vitamin reaches the body from its patch

If the company releases either, it would be worth a fresh look. Until then, any claim that the patch delivers vitamins "better than pills" or "reduces hangover symptoms" is a marketing claim, not a demonstrated result.

## The Ingredients at a Glance

Here's a quick summary of each common Bytox ingredient: why it's in there, whether it's likely to cross the skin, and what the hangover evidence looks like.

| Ingredient | Why it's included | Likely to cross skin? | Hangover evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thiamine (B1) | Heavy drinkers can become deficient | Unlikely (charged, water-soluble) | None for a single night |
| Riboflavin (B2) | Energy metabolism | Unlikely | None |
| Niacin (B3) | Building block for NAD+, used in alcohol breakdown | Possible in small amounts | Weak, from a diet survey |
| Pantothenic acid (B5) | Part of coenzyme A | Unlikely | None |
| Pyridoxine (B6) | Linked to an old pyritinol study | Possible in small amounts | Weak, old, from a related compound taken by mouth |
| Biotin (B7) | Rounds out the B-complex | Unlikely | None |
| Folate (B9) | Heavy drinkers can run low | Unlikely | None for a single night |
| Cobalamin (B12) | Popular "energy" vitamin | Very unlikely (too large) | None |

For a deeper walk through each vitamin, see the ingredient section of our [hangover patches guide](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work).

A fair note on thiamine and folate: these really do matter for people who drink heavily on a regular basis, and severe thiamine deficiency can lead to a serious brain condition called Wernicke's encephalopathy. If that describes your drinking, the answer is a conversation with your doctor and a reliable oral or injected supplement, not a sticker.

## What Users Say About Bytox

Bytox reviews on Amazon, Reddit, and elsewhere are genuinely split. We can't verify individual reviews, and star ratings move around over time, so here's a fair summary of the patterns that come up again and again rather than specific numbers.

**What people like:**

- Some people say they wake up feeling noticeably better and now use one every time they go out.
- The convenience gets a lot of praise. There's no pill to remember, and it's easy to put on before leaving the house.
- People like that it's discreet and doesn't need water or food to take.
- Fans often describe using it alongside water and a meal, as part of a routine.

**What people complain about:**

- Many reviewers say they felt no difference, especially after heavier nights.
- The patch peeling off is a very common complaint, particularly with sweat, dancing, or a shower.
- Some people get red, itchy skin from the adhesive.
- The cost per night adds up quickly compared with a bottle of B-complex tablets.
- A number of reviewers say they suspect it's placebo.

### Why some people really do feel better

It's worth taking positive reviews seriously without taking them as proof. There are several reasons someone could genuinely feel better wearing a patch that does very little:

1. **Placebo.** Expecting to feel better changes how symptoms like headache, tiredness, and low mood feel. This effect is real and can be strong.
2. **The routine effect.** Putting on a "hangover patch" is a reminder that you're trying to avoid a hangover. People who do that often drink a bit slower, eat first, and drink more water, and those habits do help.
3. **Normal variation.** Hangovers vary a lot from night to night even with similar drinking, depending on food, sleep, what you drank, and how quickly. A good morning after wearing a patch feels like proof, but it may have been a good morning anyway.
4. **Self-selection.** The people who buy and remember to wear a hangover patch are often already more careful drinkers.

None of this means people who like Bytox are wrong about how they felt. It means their experience can't separate the patch from everything else that happened that night. That's exactly the job of a placebo-controlled trial, and none has been published for Bytox.

## Bytox Pros and Cons

**Pros:**

- Very easy to use: stick it on and forget it
- Discreet, with no pills, water, or food needed
- Unlikely to cause harm in most healthy adults, mainly because little is probably absorbed
- No stomach upset, which some people get from swallowing vitamins on an empty stomach
- Can serve as a reminder to drink more carefully

**Cons:**

- No published clinical trial showing it reduces hangovers
- No published data showing how much of each vitamin reaches your blood
- B vitamins are poor candidates for skin delivery, and B12 is especially unlikely to get through
- The best comparison study found vitamin patches did worse than pills
- Expensive per night compared with an oral B-complex
- Adhesive can peel off or irritate skin
- Can create false confidence that leads to drinking more

## How Much Does Bytox Cost, and Is It Good Value?

Prices vary by pack size, retailer, and promotions, so we won't quote a specific figure that may be out of date by the time you read this. As a general guide, single-use vitamin hangover patches, Bytox included, usually work out to somewhere around one to a few dollars per patch. An ordinary oral B-complex tablet from a store brand often costs just a few cents.

Here's how the two compare on the things you can actually measure:

| | Bytox patch | Oral B-complex tablet |
|---|---|---|
| Shown to deliver vitamins to the blood | No published data | Yes, well established |
| Clinical trials for hangovers | None published | Very limited and weak |
| Rough cost per use | Around $1 to $3 | Often a few cents |
| Dose you actually get | Unknown | Close to the label amount |
| Main downsides | Peeling, skin irritation, unknown absorption | Can upset an empty stomach, bright yellow urine |
| Convenience | Very high | High (one tablet) |

If B vitamins are what you want, a tablet wins on every measurable point except a small amount of convenience. Put another way, most of what you pay for with Bytox is the delivery method, and the delivery method is the part with the least evidence behind it.

## Is Bytox Safe?

For most healthy adults, Bytox is unlikely to cause harm. The realistic risks are small but worth knowing:

- **Skin irritation or allergy.** The adhesive or any plant extracts can cause redness, itching, or a rash. Take it off if that happens, and don't put a new one on irritated or broken skin.
- **False confidence.** This is the biggest real-world risk. A patch can make people feel protected and drink more than they would have. No patch lowers your blood alcohol, speeds up how fast your liver clears alcohol, or makes it safe to drive.
- **Biotin and blood tests.** High doses of biotin can interfere with some lab tests, including certain thyroid and heart tests. Even if a patch delivers little, tell your doctor about any biotin product before blood work.
- **Stacking B6.** If you also take a multivitamin, a B-complex, and energy drinks loaded with B vitamins, it's worth being aware that very high B6 intake over long periods can cause nerve problems. A patch probably adds little, but it's another reason not to pile on products.

**Check with a doctor or pharmacist before using Bytox if** you're pregnant or breastfeeding, have eczema, psoriasis, or another skin condition, have known allergies to adhesives, or take prescription medicine.

## How to Test Bytox Fairly If You Want to Try It

If you're curious and want to try it anyway, you can get a more honest answer than most online reviews by testing it a bit more carefully:

1. **Keep everything else the same.** Compare similar nights: the same kind of drink, roughly the same amount, similar food beforehand, and similar bedtimes.
2. **Write it down the next morning.** Rate your headache, nausea, tiredness, and mood on a simple 0 to 10 scale before you think too hard about whether you wore the patch.
3. **Try several nights with and without.** One good morning proves nothing. A pattern across several nights is more meaningful, though still not a real trial.
4. **Don't change your drinking because of it.** If you drink more on patch nights, you're testing the wrong thing, and you're taking on extra risk.

If after a few honest comparisons you can't tell the difference, that's useful information, and it saves you money.

## Bytox vs Other Hangover Options

How does Bytox stack up against the other things people reach for?

- **Bytox vs other hangover patches.** Most competing patches use a very similar B-vitamin mix, so there's no evidence-based way to rank one above another. The practical differences are price, how well the adhesive sticks, and whether it bothers your skin. Our [hangover patches guide](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work) covers the category as a whole.
- **Bytox vs an oral B-complex.** Same idea, a reliable delivery route, and a fraction of the cost. If you believe B vitamins help you, this is the better way to take them.
- **Bytox vs hangover pills.** Oral hangover supplements vary widely in quality and evidence, but they avoid the skin-absorption problem entirely. Our roundup of the [best hangover pills](/never-hungover/best-hangover-pills) and our guide to [hangover supplements that actually have evidence](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025) compare the main options honestly, including where the evidence is weak.
- **Bytox vs electrolyte drinks.** Electrolyte drinks help with fluid and salt loss, which addresses one real part of a hangover (dehydration). They won't fix inflammation or poor sleep, but they're doing something measurable. See our [electrolyte drinks comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).
- **Bytox vs drinking less.** The only reliable way to avoid a hangover. Not exciting, but it works every time.

## What Actually Helps More Than a Patch

No remedy is a cure. But these steps have better support than a vitamin patch:

- **Drink less and more slowly.** Hangover severity tracks closely with how much you drink and how fast your blood alcohol rises. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that matter most.
- **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed.
- **Alternate drinks with water,** and have a glass or two before bed.
- **Choose lighter drinks.** Clear spirits like vodka and gin generally contain fewer congeners than whiskey, brandy, or red wine.
- **Protect your sleep.** Skip the last round if it's getting late, since alcohol fragments the second half of the night.
- **If you want a supplement, choose an oral one with at least some human data.** The evidence is still limited across the board, but oral products avoid the skin problem. For example, a small randomized trial published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* in 2020 found that oral L-cysteine reduced some hangover symptoms compared with placebo.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, *Hovenia dulcis*, and it's the ingredient this site focuses on. It drew attention after a 2012 study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* found it reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal in rats. Later lab and animal research has explored how it may affect alcohol metabolism and the liver.

To be straightforward: the human evidence for DHM is still limited, and there is no good evidence that it reliably prevents hangovers in everyone. We think it's a more reasonable thing to try than a vitamin patch for two reasons. It's taken by mouth, so the skin-absorption problem doesn't apply. And it's aimed at how your body handles alcohol, rather than at topping up vitamins most well-fed people aren't short of. A few newer patches list DHM, but we're not aware of any evidence that DHM crosses the skin in useful amounts, and oral products use doses of several hundred milligrams or more, far more than a patch can hold.

If you want to try it, dose and timing matter more than brand. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers typical amounts, and our [DHM timing guide](/never-hungover/when-to-take-dhm-timing-guide-2025) explains when to take it. If you want a closer look at the research, read [does DHM work?](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025). Two popular oral options are [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which pairs DHM with L-cysteine, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). (We earn a commission if you buy through these links, at no extra cost to you.)

As with any supplement, check with your doctor first if you take prescription medicine or have liver disease, and don't use DHM, a patch, or anything else as a reason to drink more.

## The Bottom Line

- **There's no good evidence that Bytox works.** The brand hasn't published a placebo-controlled hangover trial or data showing how much of its vitamins reach your blood.
- **The science of skin absorption works against it.** B vitamins are water-soluble, several are charged, and B12 is far too large to cross skin easily.
- **The best comparison study went against patches.** In a 2019 *Obesity Surgery* study, people using vitamin patches were more likely to become deficient than people taking pills.
- **B vitamins aren't a reliable hangover fix even when swallowed.** Hangovers are mostly about inflammation, acetaldehyde, poor sleep, and dehydration.
- **It's probably harmless but poor value.** The main risks are skin irritation and the false confidence to drink more.
- **Better bets:** drink less and slower, eat, hydrate, and if you want a supplement, choose an oral one with at least some human evidence.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does Bytox actually work for hangovers?**

There's no good evidence that it does. Bytox hasn't published a placebo-controlled trial showing its patch reduces hangovers, or blood data showing how much of its vitamins get through the skin. Some users say they feel better, but that can come from placebo, drinking water, eating, or simply having a lighter night.

**What's in the Bytox hangover patch?**

It's built around a B-vitamin complex: thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pantothenic acid (B5), B6, biotin (B7), folate (B9), and B12. Some versions and competing patches add extras such as vitamin C or plant extracts. Formulas change, so check the current label on the box you're buying.

**How do you use a Bytox patch?**

Stick it on clean, dry, hair-free skin, such as the inner wrist or upper arm, before you start drinking, and leave it on for several hours, typically overnight. Check the package for the exact wear time. Press it down firmly, since sweat, lotion, and showers can make it peel off.

**Can your skin absorb vitamins from a patch?**

Only to a very limited degree. Skin lets small, fat-soluble molecules through best, which is why nicotine and hormone patches work. B vitamins are water-soluble, and B12 is roughly three times the rough size limit for crossing skin. Small amounts of some vitamins may get in, but no hangover patch maker has published data showing a useful dose reaches the blood.

**Is Bytox safe?**

For most healthy adults it's unlikely to cause harm, largely because little is probably absorbed. The adhesive can irritate skin, and biotin can interfere with some blood tests, so mention it to your doctor before lab work. The bigger risk is feeling protected enough to drink more. Ask a doctor first if you're pregnant, have a skin condition, or take prescription medicine.

**Is Bytox better than taking vitamin pills?**

No. Oral B vitamins are absorbed reliably, cost a few cents, and you know roughly what dose you get. A 2019 study in Obesity Surgery found people using vitamin patches were more likely to become deficient than people taking pills. If you want B vitamins, a tablet is the better choice.

**Does Bytox lower your blood alcohol or help you sober up?**

No. Nothing in the patch affects how quickly alcohol is absorbed or cleared by your liver. Your blood alcohol level is the same with or without it, so it does not make it safe to drive or to drink more.

**Is Bytox better than DHM?**

They're very different, and neither is a guaranteed fix. Bytox delivers B vitamins through the skin, which has no published absorption data. DHM is taken by mouth and targets how the body handles alcohol, with promising animal research and limited human data. If you want to try something, an oral supplement like DHM at the right dose and timing is the more reasonable option.
